claim: Stimulus-frequency otoacoustic emissions (SFOAEs) are low-level acoustic signals recorded in response to tones that depend on active processes within the cochlea.
source: Stimulus-frequency otoacoustic emissions (SFOAEs) are low-level acoustic signals recorded in response to tones that depend on active processes within the cochlea (Kemp, 1978; Shera and Guinan, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kemp, 1978 and Shera and Guinan, 1999

claim: SFOAE delay is expected to vary with cochlear tuning sharpness based on filter theory, with longer delays implicating sharper tuning.
source: SFOAE delay is expected to vary with cochlear tuning sharpness based on filter theory, with longer delays implicating sharper tuning.
evidence: Based on established filter theory principles

claim: Previous studies found long SFOAE delays in humans, consistent with exceptional tuning sharpness.
source: Previous studies found long SFOAE delays in humans, consistent with exceptional tuning sharpness (Shera et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shera et al., 2002

claim: Behavioral tuning estimates depend on central processing of noisy signals in addition to cochlear tuning.
source: However, behavioral tuning estimates depend on central processing of noisy signals in addition to cochlear tuning, and results vary across stimulus paradigms with debate as to which methods better approximate actual tuning (Oxenham and Shera, 2003; Ruggero and Temchin, 2005; Leschke et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies discussing this issue

claim: Auditory-nerve tuning quality exceeds NSFOAE by a 'tuning ratio' that decreases from ~3 to 1 from apex to base across several species.
source: These studies found that auditory-nerve tuning quality exceeds NSFOAE (SFOAE delay in stimulus cycles) by a 'tuning ratio' that decreases from ~3 to 1 from apex to base across several species (Shera et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shera et al., 2010

claim: Only a single study has compared SFOAE and behavioral tuning estimates to auditory-nerve recordings in the same species, ferret.
source: To our knowledge, only a single study has compared SFOAE and behavioral tuning estimates to auditory-nerve recordings in the same species, ferret (Sumner et al., 2018).
evidence: Authors state this based on their knowledge of the literature

claim: SFOAE-based, behavioral, and auditory-nerve tuning quality in ferret all increased monotonically for higher frequencies, in broad accordance with one another.
source: SFOAE-based, behavioral, and auditory-nerve tuning quality in ferret all increased monotonically for higher frequencies, in broad accordance with one another (Sumner et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sumner et al., 2018

claim: The budgerigar (Melopsittacus undulatus) is a parakeet species with well-known auditory processing abilities from behavioral studies.
source: The budgerigar (Melopsittacus undulatus) is a parakeet species with well-known auditory processing abilities from behavioral studies (Dooling et al., 1989; Dooling et al., 2000; Ryals et al., 2013; Henry et al., 2016; Henry et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2019; Henry et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to behavioral studies

claim: Previous behavioral studies of critical bands and psychophysical tuning curves in budgerigars report rapidly increasing behavioral tuning sharpness with increasing frequency to a distinct peak from 3.5 to 4 kHz.
source: Intriguingly, previous behavioral studies of critical bands and psychophysical tuning curves in budgerigars report rapidly increasing behavioral tuning sharpness with increasing frequency to a distinct peak from 3.5 to 4 kHz, beyond which tuning sharpness declines dramatically (Figure 1; Saunders et al., 1978; Saunders et al., 1979; Saunders and Pallone, 1980; Dooling et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations and Figure 1 showing the data

claim: Budgerigars' average behavioral tuning Q10 increases by 2.65 dB/octave from 1 to 3.5 kHz.
source: Budgerigars' average behavioral tuning Q10 increases by 2.65 dB/octave from 1 to 3.5 kHz (i.e., nearly doubling for each octave increase; slope of 10 * log10[Q10]).
evidence: Calculated from behavioral data in the literature

claim: Slopes closer to 1 dB/octave have typically been reported in humans and various animal behavioral studies.
source: In contrast, slopes closer to 1 dB/octave have typically been reported in humans (e.g., 0.9 dB/octave; Oxenham and Shera, 2003) and various animal behavioral studies (ferret: 1.25 dB/octave in Sumner et al., 2018; macaque: 0.55 dB/octave in Burton et al., 2018; European starling: 0.95 dB/octave in Langemann et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Budgerigar critical ratios are relatively constant to 4 kHz, in contrast to other species showing 2–3 dB/octave increasing critical ratios for higher frequencies.
source: Behavioral critical ratios of the budgerigar are relatively constant to 4 kHz, in contrast to other species showing 2–3 dB/octave increasing critical ratios for higher frequencies.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1b with data from multiple species

claim: Budgerigar critical ratios diverge markedly at mid-to-high frequencies, with ~8 dB lower (more sensitive) thresholds than other bird species from 3 to 4 kHz.
source: In contrast, budgerigar critical ratios diverge markedly at mid-to-high frequencies, with ~8 dB lower (more sensitive) thresholds than other bird species from 3 to 4 kHz and intriguingly little variation in critical ratios below 4 kHz (Dooling and Saunders, 1975; Okanoya and Dooling, 1987; Farabaugh et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Constant critical ratios indicate constant bandwidth in the power spectrum model, and consequently, increasing tuning quality by 3 dB/octave.
source: Constant critical ratios indicate constant bandwidth in the power spectrum model, and consequently, increasing tuning quality by 3 dB/octave, in general agreement with budgerigars' behavioral critical bands and psychophysical tuning curves.
evidence: Based on inference from the power spectrum model

claim: Divergent critical ratios in the budgerigar occur despite similar audiogram shape in budgerigars to other avian species.
source: Notably, divergent critical ratios in the budgerigar occur despite similar audiogram shape in budgerigars to other avian species (Okanoya and Dooling, 1987; Dooling et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies comparing audiograms

claim: SFOAEs were recorded from 22 ears in 14 animals using swept-frequency tones presented at 40 dB SPL.
source: SFOAEs were recorded from 22 ears in 14 animals using swept-frequency tones presented at 40 dB SPL.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methods and sample size

claim: SFOAE level typically ranged from 5 to 15 dB at stimulus frequencies below 5–6 kHz and descended into the noise floor at higher frequencies.
source: SFOAE level (Figure 2a) typically ranged from 5 to 15 dB at stimulus frequencies below 5–6 kHz and descended into the noise floor at higher frequencies.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2a

claim: SFOAEs in individual ears typically showed three or more deep spectral notches in emission level.
source: Within the frequency of measurable emissions, SFOAEs in individual ears (Figure 2a, colored lines) typically showed three or more deep spectral notches in emission level.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2a

claim: SFOAE phase decreased monotonically with increasing frequency and was relatively consistent across individual ears.
source: SFOAE phase decreased monotonically with increasing frequency and was relatively consistent across individual ears (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2b

claim: NSFOAE increased monotonically with increasing frequency, consistent with gradually increasing tuning quality along the length of the cochlea from apex to base.
source: So calculated, NSFOAE increased monotonically with increasing frequency, consistent with gradually increasing tuning quality along the length of the cochlea from apex to base.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2c and inference about cochlear tuning

claim: Linear mixed-effects modeling revealed a significant effect of frequency on SFOAE level (F4,84 = 18.91, p<0.0001).
source: Linear mixed-effects modeling revealed a significant effect of frequency on SFOAE level (F4,84 = 18.91, p<0.0001), associated with slightly lower SFOAE level in the higher frequency bands (see Materials and methods: Statistical analysis).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: A linear mixed-model analysis of NSFOAE revealed a significant effect of frequency (F4,84 = 44.05, p<0.0001) due to greater NSFOAE in higher frequency bands.
source: Moreover, a linear mixed-model analysis of NSFOAE revealed a significant effect of frequency (F4,84 = 44.05, p<0.0001) due to greater NSFOAE in higher frequency bands.
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The mean rate of increase in NSFOAE was 1.65 dB/octave.
source: The mean rate of increase in NSFOAE was 1.65 dB/octave.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data

claim: Auditory-nerve tuning curves (n=127) in budgerigars had CFs ranging from 0.28 to 5.65 kHz.
source: Auditory-nerve tuning curves (n=127) in budgerigars had CFs ranging from 0.28 to 5.65 kHz (median: 2.97 kHz; interquartile range: 1.13–3.88 kHz) and associated thresholds at CF as low as 5 dB SPL (Figure 3a, crosses).
evidence: Direct measurement from experimental data

claim: Individual tuning curves appeared symmetric around CF on a log-frequency axis, with no clear indication of a secondary tail region of low-frequency sensitivity for stimulus levels up to 80 dB SPL.
source: Individual tuning curves (Figure 3a, colored lines) appeared symmetric around CF on a log-frequency axis, with no clear indication of a secondary tail region of low-frequency sensitivity for stimulus levels up to 80 dB SPL (i.e., the highest level tested).
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figure 3a

claim: Q10 increased monotonically and significantly for higher CFs (t125=6.542, p<0.0001).
source: Q10, the measure of tuning-curve sharpness, increased monotonically and significantly for higher CFs (Figure 3b; t125=6.542, p<0.0001; t-test of linear regression slope between log-transformed variables) as in other animal species, without an apparent peak at 3.5–4 kHz.
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The rate of increase for Q10 with increasing frequency was 0.87 dB/octave.
source: The rate of increase for Q10 with increasing frequency was 0.87 dB/octave, that is, lower than the 1.65 dB/octave rate observed for NSFOAE (Figure 3b; red line) and considerably lower than the 2.65 dB/octave rate for the behavioral literature (Figure 1; see below for further comparison).
evidence: Calculated from experimental data

claim: QERB exceeded Q10 by a median factor of 1.76 (interquartile range: 1.65–1.89).
source: QERB also increased monotonically for higher CFs (see below) and exceeded Q10 by a median factor of 1.76 (interquartile range: 1.65–1.89).
evidence: Calculated from experimental data

claim: The tuning ratio r is defined as the quotient of auditory-nerve QERB and NSFOAE.
source: Previous studies (e.g., Shera et al., 2002; Shera et al., 2010) established the concept of a tuning ratio, r, assumed to vary slowly with frequency and fit to the empirically derived quotient of auditory-nerve QERB and NSFOAE, as indicated in Equation 1.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies defining this concept

claim: The value of r in mammals decreases from ~3 at the apical end of the cochlea to 1 for frequencies processed more basally.
source: The value of r in mammals decreases from ~3 at the apical end of the cochlea to 1 for frequencies processed more basally (Shera et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shera et al., 2010

claim: Multiplying NSFOAE by r from a different species or species group accurately predicts auditory-nerve QERB in many cases.
source: r appears largely conserved across related species, such that multiplying NSFOAE by r from a different species or species group accurately predicts auditory-nerve QERB in many cases (Shera et al., 2010; Joris et al., 2011; Sumner et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Chicken data were selected rather than barn owl due to greater similarity of the chicken's cochlear morphology and frequency limits of hearing to budgerigar.
source: Chicken data were selected rather than barn owl (Tyto alba; Bergevin et al., 2015) due to greater similarity of the chicken's cochlear morphology (Gleich and Manley, 2000) and frequency limits of hearing (chicken: 9.1–7,200 Hz [Hill et al., 2014]; budgerigar: 77–7,600 Hz [Heffner et al., 2016]; frequency ranges for which behavioral audiometric thresholds are less than 60 dB SPL).
evidence: Reasoning based on cited morphological and hearing data

claim: Auditory-nerve Q10 from two previous chicken studies increases monotonically for higher frequencies.
source: Auditory-nerve Q10 from two previous chicken studies (Manley et al., 1991; Saunders et al., 1996) increases monotonically for higher frequencies (Figure 4a).
evidence: Based on data from cited studies shown in Figure 4a

claim: NSFOAE in chicken increases monotonically for higher frequencies, similar to the pattern observed for auditory-nerve Q10.
source: NSFOAE in chicken also increases monotonically for higher frequencies (Bergevin et al., 2008; Figure 4a, red line), similar to the pattern observed for auditory-nerve Q10.
evidence: Based on data from cited study shown in Figure 4a

claim: Chicken r decreased from a maximum value of ~7 at 500 Hz to 3–4 at frequencies from 1 to 3.35 kHz.
source: Chicken r decreased from a maximum value of ~7 at 500 Hz to 3–4 at frequencies from 1 to 3.35 kHz.
evidence: Calculated from chicken data shown in Figure 4b

claim: Empirical evaluation of chicken r was limited to frequencies less than 3.35 kHz due to the scala tympani approach of the two auditory-nerve studies.
source: Note that empirical evaluation of chicken r was limited to frequencies less than 3.35 kHz due to the scala tympani approach of the two auditory-nerve studies, which limited sampling from high-CF fibers (Manley et al., 1991; Saunders et al., 1996).
evidence: Based on methodological limitations described in cited studies

claim: Budgerigar r was marginally lower than that of chickens and followed the same trajectory with increasing frequency, decreasing from a maximum of ~4 at 700 Hz to ~2 at 5.5 kHz.
source: Finally, budgerigar r was calculated using the same empirical method, but without extrapolation due to broad sampling of CFs with our auditory-nerve approach. Budgerigar r was marginally lower than that of chickens and followed the same trajectory with increasing frequency, decreasing from a maximum of ~4 at 700 Hz to ~2 at 5.5 kHz (Figure 4b, thick black line).
evidence: Calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 4b

claim: SFOAE-based predictions of cochlear tuning in budgerigars were made by multiplying NSFOAE by chicken r as a function of frequency.
source: SFOAE-based predictions of cochlear tuning in budgerigars were made by multiplying NSFOAE by chicken r as a function of frequency (Figure 5; magenta).
evidence: Description of analysis method shown in Figure 5

claim: NSFOAE predictions made using both the empirical and extended-frequency forms of chicken r reasonably approximated budgerigar auditory-nerve QERB measurements.
source: Whereas NSFOAE predictions made using both the empirical and extended-frequency forms of chicken r reasonably approximated budgerigar auditory-nerve QERB measurements, running parallel to and slightly above the mean trendline, the behavioral results show a fundamentally different pattern characterized by a noticeably greater slope from 0.5 to 3.5 kHz, distinct peak from 3.5 to 4 kHz, and steep roll off above 4 kHz.
evidence: Comparison of predictions to data shown in Figure 5

claim: SFOAE results provided closer estimates of actual auditory-nerve QERB than did behaviorally estimated tuning measures in the budgerigar.
source: Thus, SFOAE results provided closer estimates of actual auditory-nerve QERB than did behaviorally estimated tuning measures in the budgerigar, and we find no evidence that unusual behavioral tuning in budgerigars arises peripherally.
evidence: Inference from comparison of SFOAE predictions and behavioral data to auditory-nerve measurements

claim: There is no evidence that unusual behavioral tuning in budgerigars arises peripherally.
source: Thus, SFOAE results provided closer estimates of actual auditory-nerve QERB than did behaviorally estimated tuning measures in the budgerigar, and we find no evidence that unusual behavioral tuning in budgerigars arises peripherally.
evidence: Inference from comparison of peripheral measures (SFOAE and auditory-nerve) to behavioral data

claim: SFOAE delay expressed as NSFOAE increases for higher frequencies in a wide range of taxa, in qualitative agreement with patterns of auditory-nerve tuning quality in these species.
source: SFOAE delay expressed as NSFOAE increases for higher frequencies in a wide range of taxa, in qualitative agreement with patterns of auditory-nerve tuning quality in these species (macaque monkeys: Joris et al., 2011; chinchilla: Shera et al., 2010; gecko: Bergevin and Shera, 2010; cat and guinea pig: Shera et al., 2002; ferret: Sumner et al., 2018; chicken: Bergevin et al., 2008; barn owl: Bergevin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies across species

claim: In the budgerigar, use of r from chicken predicted auditory-nerve QERB with good quantitative precision across the full range of frequencies evaluated.
source: In the budgerigar, use of r from chicken predicted auditory-nerve QERB with good quantitative precision across the full range of frequencies evaluated (Figure 5).
evidence: Comparison of predictions to data shown in Figure 5

claim: The precision of SFOAE predictions is attributable to similarity of r between the budgerigar and chicken.
source: The precision of SFOAE predictions is attributable to similarity of r between the budgerigar and chicken (Figure 4b).
evidence: Inference from comparison of r values shown in Figure 4b

claim: The value of r in barn owl ranges from 1 to 2.
source: The value of r in mammals decreases from ~3 to 1 from apex to base (Shera et al., 2010), whereas r in the barn owl ranges from 1 to 2 (Bergevin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bergevin et al., 2015

claim: Differences in hearing sensitivity could be one factor contributing to species differences in r.
source: The reasons for species differences in r are unknown, though level dependence of r in previous studies suggests that differences in hearing sensitivity could be one factor (Bergevin et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculation based on cited study showing level dependence

claim: Mammalian studies suggest an apical-basal transition point for r, basal to which r approaches ~1 and apical to which r varies inversely with frequency.
source: Moreover, mammalian studies suggest an apical-basal transition point for r, basal to which r approaches ~1 and apical to which r varies inversely with frequency (Shera et al., 2010; Shera and Charaziak, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to mammalian studies

claim: Whether an apical-basal transition occurs in the avian cochlea is unknown.
source: Whether an apical-basal transition occurs in the avian cochlea is unknown, but it is intriguing to note that r from the budgerigar and chicken shows some resemblance to the apical portion of r in cat, guinea pig, chinchilla, and probably other mammalian species (Shera et al., 2010; Shera and Charaziak, 2019).
evidence: Authors state this is unknown based on their knowledge

claim: Measurements of chicken auditory-nerve tuning were drawn from two previously published studies and were limited to CFs less than 3.35 kHz due to their recording methodology.
source: Measurements of chicken auditory-nerve tuning were drawn from two previously published studies and were limited to CFs less than 3.35 kHz due to their recording methodology (Manley et al., 1991; Saunders et al., 1996).
evidence: Based on methodological limitations described in cited studies

claim: CFs likely exist up to at least 5 kHz in chicken based on the chicken's behavioral audiogram.
source: CFs likely exist up to at least 5 kHz based on the chicken's behavioral audiogram (Hill et al., 2014), but were not sampled due to the scala tympani approach employed by these studies (Manley et al., 1991; Saunders et al., 1996).
evidence: Inference based on cited behavioral audiogram data

claim: The estimates of behavioral frequency selectivity referenced in the present study were originally obtained using three simultaneous masking paradigms: psychophysical tuning curves, critical bands, and critical ratios.
source: The estimates of behavioral frequency selectivity referenced in the present study were originally obtained using three simultaneous masking paradigms: psychophysical tuning curves for probe-tone detection in tonal or narrowband maskers, critical bands for tone detection in bandlimited noise, and critical ratios for tone detection in wideband noise (Dooling and Saunders, 1975; Saunders et al., 1978; Saunders et al., 1979; Saunders and Pallone, 1980; Kuhn and Saunders, 1980; Dooling et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to the original behavioral studies

claim: All three behavioral measures show that perceptual frequency selectivity in budgerigars is greatest from 3.5 to 4 kHz and declines markedly at higher and lower frequencies.
source: All three behavioral measures show that perceptual frequency selectivity in budgerigars is greatest from 3.5 to 4 kHz and declines markedly at higher and lower frequencies.
evidence: Summary of behavioral data from cited studies

claim: Neither SFOAEs nor auditory-nerve recordings suggest the existence of a peripheral auditory specialization that could explain prior behavioral findings in budgerigars.
source: Critically, the behavioral findings contrast with physiological tuning estimates of the current study, which show monotonically increasing SFOAE phase gradients with increasing frequency as well as monotonically increasing auditory-nerve Q10/QERB values for higher CFs. Thus, neither SFOAEs nor auditory-nerve recordings suggest the existence of a peripheral auditory specialization that could explain prior behavioral findings in this species.
evidence: Inference from comparison of current physiological data to behavioral data

claim: Forward-masking procedures are hypothesized to more accurately predict cochlear frequency tuning in humans.
source: Forward-masking procedures are hypothesized to more accurately predict cochlear frequency tuning in humans (Shera et al., 2002; Joris et al., 2011; Sumner et al., 2018), but evidence from nonhuman studies is mixed.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies proposing this hypothesis

claim: Sumner et al., 2018 found that forward-masking behavioral results better predicted auditory-nerve tuning than simultaneous masking in the ferret.
source: Sumner et al., 2018 found that forward-masking behavioral results better predicted auditory-nerve tuning than simultaneous masking in the ferret (Sumner et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sumner et al., 2018

claim: Ruggero and Temchin, 2005 argued that forward-masking behavioral paradigms can substantially overestimate cochlear frequency selectivity.
source: On the other hand, Ruggero and Temchin, 2005 argued that forward-masking behavioral paradigms can substantially overestimate cochlear frequency selectivity, highlighting several cases where simultaneous-masking procedures produce close quantitative predictions of auditory-nerve tuning (e.g., guinea pig, chinchilla, macaque; Ruggero and Temchin, 2005; see Joris et al., 2011 for macaque auditory-nerve tuning).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruggero and Temchin, 2005

claim: In budgerigars, psychophysical tuning curves obtained with pure-tone forward masking have Q10 values that are greater than twice simultaneous-masking values at the same frequencies.
source: Interestingly in the budgerigar, psychophysical tuning curves obtained with pure-tone forward masking Kuhn and Saunders, 1980 have Q10 values that are greater than twice simultaneous-masking values at the same frequencies (Figure 1; red triangles), while also far exceeding (by two- or threefold) the maximum auditory-nerve Q10 values reported in Figure 3.
evidence: Comparison of data from cited study to current data shown in Figures 1 and 3

claim: Behavioral measures of frequency selectivity necessarily involve the entire auditory pathway and central nervous system, including neural mechanisms for processing masked signals.
source: However, behavioral measures of frequency selectivity necessarily involve the entire auditory pathway and central nervous system, including neural mechanisms for processing masked signals, and are best explained by models that include both peripheral and central auditory system processes (Maxwell et al., 2020; Brennan et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to modeling studies

claim: The unique pattern observed in the budgerigar's behavioral Q10 trendline may reflect specializations for masked processing in the central auditory pathway of this highly vocal and gregarious species.
source: The unique pattern observed in the budgerigar's behavioral Q10 trendline may then reflect specializations for masked processing in the central auditory pathway of this highly vocal and gregarious species.
evidence: Speculation based on the mismatch between behavioral and peripheral measures

claim: The frequency selectivity of inferior colliculus response maps obtained with single tones showed no obvious peak in tuning quality for neural CFs from 3.5 to 4 kHz.
source: Note that the frequency selectivity of inferior colliculus response maps obtained with single tones of varying frequency and level showed no obvious peak in tuning quality for neural CFs from 3.5 to 4 kHz (Henry et al., 2016; Henry et al., 2017), similar to the present auditory-nerve results.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Several histological studies of budgerigar cochlear morphology revealed no obvious specializations consistent with a peripheral auditory specialization.
source: Finally, several histological studies of budgerigar cochlear morphology also revealed no obvious specializations consistent with a peripheral auditory specialization (Manley et al., 1993; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to histological studies

claim: SFOAE-based and auditory-nerve measures of tuning sharpness increased for higher frequencies in the budgerigars.
source: In conclusion, SFOAE-based and auditory-nerve measures of tuning sharpness increased for higher frequencies in the budgerigars, and quantitative SFOAE predictions based on r from a different bird species (chicken) closely approximated actual budgerigar auditory-nerve tuning.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Quantitative SFOAE predictions based on r from chicken closely approximated actual budgerigar auditory-nerve tuning.
source: In conclusion, SFOAE-based and auditory-nerve measures of tuning sharpness increased for higher frequencies in the budgerigars, and quantitative SFOAE predictions based on r from a different bird species (chicken) closely approximated actual budgerigar auditory-nerve tuning.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: The pattern of SFOAE and auditory-nerve tuning in budgerigars is similar to findings in other avian and mammalian species.
source: The pattern is similar to findings in other avian and mammalian species and contrasts with the unusual pattern of behavioral frequency tuning in budgerigars, which has maximum tuning quality from 3.5 to 4 kHz consistent with an auditory specialization.
evidence: Comparison to literature on other species

claim: These results highlight the need for caution in interpreting behavioral measures of frequency tuning.
source: These results highlight the need for caution in interpreting behavioral measures of frequency tuning, which can show substantial deviation from cochlear tuning curves due to central processing mechanisms and other factors that necessarily influence behavioral detection of masked signals.
evidence: Inference from the findings of the study

claim: Behavioral measures of frequency tuning can show substantial deviation from cochlear tuning curves due to central processing mechanisms and other factors that necessarily influence behavioral detection of masked signals.
source: These results highlight the need for caution in interpreting behavioral measures of frequency tuning, which can show substantial deviation from cochlear tuning curves due to central processing mechanisms and other factors that necessarily influence behavioral detection of masked signals.
evidence: Inference from the findings of the study

claim: SFOAEs were recorded from 22 ears in 14 budgerigars (7 female).
source: SFOAEs were recorded from 22 ears in 14 budgerigars (7 female).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental sample

claim: Birds used for SFOAE recordings were 6–32 months old with a median age of 8.5 months.
source: Birds were 6–32 months old with a median age of 8.5 months at the time of SFOAE experiments.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental sample characteristics

claim: Auditory-nerve responses were recorded from six ears in six budgerigars (four females).
source: Auditory-nerve responses were recorded from six ears in six budgerigars (four females).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental sample

claim: Birds used for auditory-nerve recordings were 6–22 months old at the time of the recordings (median: 7.5 months).
source: Birds were 6–22 months old at the time of the auditory-nerve recordings (median: 7.5 months).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental sample characteristics

claim: All experiments were approved by the University of Rochester Committee on Animal Resources (UCAR-2011-015).
source: All experiments were approved by the University of Rochester Committee on Animal Resources (UCAR-2011-015).
evidence: Statement of ethical approval

claim: Animals were anesthetized for SFOAE recordings by subcutaneous injection of 0.08–0.12 mg/kg dexmedetomidine and 3–5.8 mg/kg ketamine.
source: Animals were anesthetized for SFOAE recordings by subcutaneous injection of 0.08–0.12 mg/kg dexmedetomidine and 3–5.8 mg/kg ketamine.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Temperature was maintained at 40℃ throughout the SFOAE experiment using a feedback-controlled heating pad.
source: Temperature was maintained at 40℃ throughout the experiment using a feedback-controlled heating pad (Harvard Apparatus Model 50-753, Edenbridge, KY, USA).
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Careful control of temperature was found to be critical for robust emission measurements.
source: Careful control of temperature was found to be critical for robust emission measurements.
evidence: Observation from experimental experience

claim: The probe for SFOAE recordings consisted of a tone linearly swept at a constant rate from 500 Hz to 8 kHz over 2.05 s, presented at 40 dB SPL.
source: The probe consisted of a tone linearly swept at a constant rate from 500 Hz to 8 kHz over 2.05 s, presented at 40 dB SPL.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: The suppressor for SFOAE recordings consisted of a tone swept at a constant rate from 540 Hz to 8.04 kHz over 2.05 s, presented at 55 dB SPL.
source: The suppressor consisted of a tone swept at a constant rate from 540 Hz to 8.04 kHz over 2.05 s, presented at 55 dB SPL.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Each SFOAE experiment consisted of 40 repetitions of the stimulus sequence.
source: Each experiment consisted of 40 repetitions of the stimulus sequence.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: PSFOAE was calculated by vector subtraction of the response waveforms.
source: PSFOAE was calculated by vector subtraction (Shera et al., 2002), as indicated in Equation 2, where P is the response waveform in Pa and subscripts denote the stimulus class.
evidence: Description of analysis method with citation

claim: The noise floor was estimated by the spectrum of the difference between odd and even trials of SFOAEs.
source: The noise floor was estimated by the spectrum of the difference between odd and even trials of SFOAEs.
evidence: Description of analysis method

claim: Data points less than 10 dB in magnitude above the median of the estimated noise floor were rejected prior to phase-gradient extraction.
source: Data points less than 10 dB in magnitude above the median of the estimated noise floor were rejected.
evidence: Description of data exclusion criteria

claim: Data points at the base of magnitude troughs were rejected due to noted phase irregularities.
source: Data points at the base of magnitude troughs were also rejected due to noted phase irregularities.
evidence: Description of data exclusion criteria based on observation

claim: CF was calculated as the frequency of the lowest threshold in auditory-nerve tuning curves.
source: CF was calculated as the frequency of the lowest threshold, Q10 was calculated as CF divided by the tuning curve bandwidth 10 dB above the lowest threshold, and QERB (i.e., the tuning quality of the idealized rectangular filter with equivalent bandwidth to the measured tuning curve) was calculated based on the area under the inverted tuning curve, as in Bergevin et al., 2015.
evidence: Description of analysis method

claim: Q10 was calculated as CF divided by the tuning curve bandwidth 10 dB above the lowest threshold.
source: CF was calculated as the frequency of the lowest threshold, Q10 was calculated as CF divided by the tuning curve bandwidth 10 dB above the lowest threshold, and QERB (i.e., the tuning quality of the idealized rectangular filter with equivalent bandwidth to the measured tuning curve) was calculated based on the area under the inverted tuning curve, as in Bergevin et al., 2015.
evidence: Description of analysis method

claim: QERB was calculated based on the area under the inverted tuning curve.
source: CF was calculated as the frequency of the lowest threshold, Q10 was calculated as CF divided by the tuning curve bandwidth 10 dB above the lowest threshold, and QERB (i.e., the tuning quality of the idealized rectangular filter with equivalent bandwidth to the measured tuning curve) was calculated based on the area under the inverted tuning curve, as in Bergevin et al., 2015.
evidence: Description of analysis method with citation

claim: Linear mixed-effects models were implemented to determine the effect of frequency on SFOAE magnitude and phase-gradient responses.
source: Linear mixed-effects models were implemented to determine the effect of frequency on SFOAE magnitude and phase-gradient responses.
evidence: Description of statistical analysis method
